---
title: "Social work: Missed appointments"
---

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
**Domain:** Social work — case assessment
:::

## Teaching task

> A client receiving substance-use counselling has missed three appointments in a row. What would you consider before reaching out, and how would you frame the contact?

## Calibrated student responses

### Response A — `extrinsic_distractor`

> First I would check the file to see if any documentation is overdue, and make sure the client's intake forms are complete in our system. Then I'd verify the contact information is current and check whether their insurance authorization is still active. After that I'd update the case notes to record that contact is pending.

::: {.callout-feedback}
**Why this is `extrinsic_distractor`:** the student spends their cognitive effort on agency-process tasks (forms, billing, notes) instead of the substantive question (the client's wellbeing and engagement). Effort goes to the wrong place.
:::

### Response B — `active_misconception`

> Three missed appointments means the client isn't taking their recovery seriously. I would call them and remind them of their commitments and explain that if they miss another one we may have to close the case. We can't help people who don't show up.

::: {.callout-feedback}
**Why this is `active_misconception`:** the student reasons coherently from a wrong model (client = autonomous decision-maker who is choosing not to comply). The model needs replacing, not refining: structural and clinical factors are entirely outside the frame.
:::

### Response C — `intrinsic_overload`

> There could be many reasons: relapse, transportation, work schedule, mental health, family crisis, housing instability, stigma, fear of judgment, distrust of the agency, transportation costs, childcare, language barriers, immigration status concerns, conflict with previous staff, perceived lack of progress, or just feeling overwhelmed by the process itself.

::: {.callout-feedback}
**Why this is `intrinsic_overload`:** the student tracks many real and relevant possibilities but cannot prioritise or move from list to action. The element-interactivity exceeds working-memory capacity, so analysis collapses into enumeration.
:::
